analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal Public Advocate office to represent ordinary people in FERC energy proceedings.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or a cosponsor before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of Public Advocate inside the Department of Justice to represent members of the public in matters before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). It would collect comments from people and local governments affected by proposed energy projects, submit them to FERC with recommendations, check whether project applicants obey FERC orders, and go to court when noncompliance or a FERC order harms people's health, safety, or welfare. Congress found that FERC was not adequately informing property owners and local officials and did not give states and localities enough say in project approvals.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners, local governments, and other members of the public who live near or are affected by energy projects approved by FERC, such as pipelines, power plants, and transmission lines. The bill itself notes that landowners and local officials often do not understand their rights during FERC's certificate application process and have little chance to participate [S3]. The office would give them a funded federal representative for free, rather than requiring them to hire lawyers to face well-resourced energy companies in FERC proceedings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Property owners near FERC-regulated energy projects

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Public Advocate in the Department of Justice to represent the interests of members of the public affected by FERC matters, including in other federal agencies and in court [S3].

Requires the office to receive and assess comments from all interested parties on project applications before FERC — including individuals, municipalities, counties, and states — and submit them to FERC with findings and recommendations on the outcome, terms, and conditions of approval [S2].

Requires the office to review applicant compliance with FERC orders, seek full compliance when noncompliance harms the health, safety, or welfare of affected parties, and, at its discretion, appeal FERC orders it deems harmful to affected parties [S2].

Congress's findings in the bill state that FERC does not adequately inform property owners and local officials about the application process, that states and localities lack adequate participation, and that local environmental resources lack adequate protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund a new federal office within the Department of Justice, including staff who review applications, monitor compliance, and litigate. Energy companies seeking FERC approval for projects would face an additional official adversary reviewing their applications, monitoring their compliance with orders, and potentially appealing approvals they receive, which could add time and cost to permitting.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new federal office with no dedicated funding mechanism specified in the text, so its cost to taxpayers would depend entirely on future appropriations decisions [S3].

By formally opposing or appealing project approvals and demanding stronger compliance, the office could slow approvals for energy infrastructure such as pipelines and transmission lines; slower permitting raises project costs that can be passed through to energy customers [S3].

The bill gives the office sole discretion over which FERC orders to appeal and which comments to elevate, concentrating significant judgment in one office within the Justice Department without specified qualification or review standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but hard to quantify: people facing a large energy project would have a federal advocate representing their interests at no cost to them, in a process the bill's own findings describe as inadequate for property owners and local officials. The costs are a new federal office and the possibility of slower, more contested FERC permitting for energy projects — which cuts both ways, since it protects affected communities but can delay infrastructure. The design is skeletal: no funding, staffing, or qualification standards are specified, so the office's real-world impact would depend entirely on how future administrations funded and ran it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, then to subcommittees in each, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Gerlach introduced the bill on May 3, 2011 [S1].
The House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power on May 6, 2011, and to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law on August 25, 2011 [S5].
The bill never advanced beyond subcommittee referral and attracted no cosponsors before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy companies and project applicants before FERC, who faced no new federal advocate scrutinizing their applications or enforcing orders against them. Property owners and communities near proposed pipelines and other FERC-regulated projects gained nothing, and continued to bear their own costs to participate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy applicants before FERC, untouched by it

for.name: Rep. Jim Gerlach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and the findings that FERC shortchanges property owners, local officials, and state participation in project approvals [S1][S3].

against.name: Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee (112th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or the floor; no action followed the subcommittee referral [S5].

against.name: Lamar Smith
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or the floor; no action followed [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other member signed on, so there is no record of where members beyond the sponsor stood; the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Energy project developers (pipelines, power plants, transmission) regulated by FERC
industries.note: The bill would put a federal advocate on the other side of every project application, monitoring compliance with FERC orders and appealing approvals that harm affected parties. Developers currently face only the applicants' own resources in most proceedings, which is a structural advantage the bill would erode.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and natural gas utilities
industries.note: Firms holding FERC certificates would face stricter scrutiny of their compliance with commission orders, which protects communities but can raise their costs. The bill does not change their market position, only the oversight around them.
